facts.fact: The repository contains code to produce Election Galton Boards.
facts.quote: This repository contains code to produce Election Galton Boards

facts.fact: Election Galton Boards are Galton boards that roughly approximate predictive distributions.
facts.quote: Galton boards that roughly approximate the predictive distributions for the 2020 US President electoral college vote

facts.fact: The approximations are based on different poll aggregators.
facts.quote: predictive distributions for the 2020 US President electoral college vote, according to different poll aggregators.

facts.fact: The boards can be seen in action at presidential-plinko.com.
facts.quote: You can see them in action at [presidential-plinko.com](http://presidential-plinko.com/).

facts.fact: The Galton boards are based on models from 538 and the Economist.
facts.quote: The Galton boards are based on the models of [538]

facts.fact: The modelers open their election forecast data.
facts.quote: both of which are nice enough to open their data.

facts.fact: Running build.R downloads the latest model versions and re-renders everything.
facts.quote: To download the latest versions of the Economist's and 538's models and re-render everything, run [build.R](build.R).

facts.fact: The code determines binomial approximations to each modeler's predictions and builds the Plinko boards.
facts.quote: The code for determining the binomial approximations to each modeler's predictions and then building the Plinko boards is in [binomial_approx_both.md]

facts.fact: An experimental plinko R package is used to construct animated Plinko boards.
facts.quote: It uses my experimental [plinko](https://mjskay.github.io/plinko/) R package for constructing animated Plinko boards.

facts.fact: Older pre-plinko code for building the Galton boards is in galton_board_quantile_ragg.Rmd.
facts.quote: An older version of the code (pre-[plinko](https://mjskay.github.io/plinko/)) for building the Galton boards is in [galton_board_quantile_ragg.Rmd]

facts.fact: The library draws bumps charts using d3.
facts.quote: Draw Bumps charts using d3.

facts.fact: It supports AMD, CommonJS, and vanilla environments.
facts.quote: AMD, CommonJS, and vanilla environments are supported.

facts.fact: In vanilla usage, a d3 global is exported.
facts.quote: In vanilla, a `d3` global is exported:

facts.fact: A bumps chart generator is constructed with default settings.
facts.quote: Constructs a new bumps chart generator with the default settings.

facts.fact: The chart is rendered to a given selection.
facts.quote: Render the bumps chart to the given _[selection](https://github.com/d3/d3-selection)_.

facts.fact: The year range is configured with start and end values.
facts.quote: .year({ start: 2014, end: 2017 })

facts.fact: Window width can be set from the document body client width.
facts.quote: .windowWidth(window.document.body.clientWidth)

facts.fact: A selectYear event fires after the year range has changed.
facts.quote: `selectYear` - after the year range has changed.

facts.fact: A toggleSelectedCrew event fires after a crew's selected status has been toggled.
facts.quote: `toggleSelectedCrew` - after a crew's selected status has been toggled.

facts.fact: A highlightCrew event fires after the highlighted crew has changed.
facts.quote: `highlightCrew` - after the highlighted crew has changed.

facts.fact: The on method sets an event listener for specified typenames.
facts.quote: If _listener_ is specified, sets the event _listener_ for the specified _typenames_ and returns the bumps chart.

facts.fact: The example filters events by gender.
facts.quote: .filter(e => e.gender.toLowerCase() === gender.toLowerCase())

facts.fact: The example filters events by set.
facts.quote: .filter(e => e.set === set)

facts.fact: The example sorts events by year and maps each through transformData.
facts.quote:
.sort((a, b) => a.year - b.year)
      .map(event => d3.transformData(event))

facts.fact: Transformed events are joined with joinEvents using set and gender.
facts.quote: var data = d3.joinEvents(transformedEvents, set, gender);

facts.fact: The project is a replication of Stake.com's Plinko game.
facts.quote: This project is a replication of [Stake.com's Plinko game](https://stake.com/casino/games/plinko)

facts.fact: Plinko mechanics drop a ball through a multi-row pin pyramid into payout bins at the bottom.
facts.quote: Plinko is a classic game where the player drops a ball in a multi-row pin pyramid, where the ball bounces randomly until it reaches the payout bins at the bottom.

facts.fact: The implementation uses Svelte, Tailwind CSS, and matter-js.
facts.quote: created using [Svelte](https://svelte.dev/), [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/), and [matter-js](https://github.com/liabru/matter-js).

facts.fact: matter-js is used as the physics engine.
facts.quote: This is because this project uses [matter-js](https://github.com/liabru/matter-js) as the physics engine.

facts.fact: Outcomes are calculated client-side, so they cannot be pre-determined before the ball drop.
facts.quote: this project calculates the outcome on the client-side, so we cannot pre-determine the outcome before ball drop

facts.fact: Because the physics engine runs client-side, the outcome is unknown until the ball reaches the bottom.
facts.quote: This engine runs on client-side, so the outcome is unknown until the ball reaches the bottom.

facts.fact: Stake.com instead calculates the outcome on a back-end server and drops the ball to the determined pin.
facts.quote: This is different from Stake.com's implementation, where they calculate the outcome in a back-end server, then drop the ball to the determined pin.

facts.fact: Physics-engine unpredictability can make actual average return higher than expected value, sometimes positive.
facts.quote: Due to the physics engine's unpredictability, the actual average return value may be higher than the expected value (sometimes positive return).

facts.fact: The UI/gameplay supports manual and auto-bet modes.
facts.quote: Manual and auto-bet modes

facts.fact: The game displays real-time live stats.
facts.quote: Real-time live stats

facts.fact: The UI is described as responsive.
facts.quote: Responsive design

facts.fact: The game is free to play and lets players add money at any time.
facts.quote: 100% free to play, add money at any time

facts.fact: A hidden local-development page benchmarks payout probabilities and expected values.
facts.quote: A hidden page is only available in local dev environment to benchmark the payout probabilities and expected values.

facts.fact: The benchmark page was used to tune matter-js physics parameters and control expected payout.
facts.quote: I used this page to tune the parameters of the matter-js physics engine and control the expected payout.

facts.fact: The project keeps Stake.com's original payout table.
facts.quote: I stick to the original Stake.com's payout table for simplicity.

facts.fact: Matter.js is a JavaScript 2D rigid body physics engine for the web.
facts.quote: *Matter.js* is a JavaScript 2D rigid body physics engine for the web

facts.fact: The engine supports concave and convex hulls.
facts.quote: - Concave and convex hulls

facts.fact: Bodies have physical properties such as mass, area, and density.
facts.quote: - Physical properties (mass, area, density etc.)

facts.fact: Restitution supports elastic and inelastic collisions.
facts.quote: - Restitution (elastic and inelastic collisions)

facts.fact: Collision detection includes broad-phase, mid-phase, and narrow-phase.
facts.quote: - Collisions (broad-phase, mid-phase and narrow-phase)

facts.fact: The engine provides stable stacking and resting.
facts.quote: - Stable stacking and resting

facts.fact: Friction and resistance are simulated.
facts.quote: - Friction and resistance

facts.fact: Sleeping and static bodies are supported.
facts.quote: - Sleeping and static bodies

facts.fact: Rounded corners can be chamfered.
facts.quote: - Rounded corners (chamfering)

facts.fact: The canvas renderer supports vectors and textures.
facts.quote: - Canvas renderer (supports vectors and textures)

facts.fact: Time scaling supports slow-motion and speed-up.
facts.quote: - Time scaling (slow-mo, speed-up)
